claims.text: What the image looks like LA mass attached to the fossa ovalis, ball-on-stalk → atrial myxoma
claims.quote: LA mass attached to fossa ovalis, ball-on-stalk Atrial myxoma

claims.text: Example cardiac CTA: a left atrial mass attached by a stalk to the interatrial septum, an appearance typical of atrial myxoma
claims.quote: This CTA shows a left atrial mass attached by a stalk to the interatrial septum, an appearance that is typical of atrial myxoma.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Chamber sizes: LV (LVEDD, LVESD), RV (> 1:1 with LV = dilated), LA, RA
claims.quote: Chamber sizes - LV (LVEDD, LVESD), RV (>1:1 with LV = dilated), LA, RA.

claims.text: TEE is better for atrial tumors and TTE for ventricular tumors; echo is the modality of choice for very mobile tumors, particularly small ones
claims.quote: Transesophageal echocardiography is better for visualizing atrial tumors, and transthoracic echocardiography is better for ventricular tumors. Due to its superior temporal resolution, echocardiography is the imaging modality of choice in visualizing very mobile cardiac tumors, particularly when they are small.

claims.text: Cardiac MRI: a left atrial myxoma hyperintense on T2-weighted image, an appearance typical of myxoma
claims.quote: This cardiac MRI shows a left atrial myxoma (arrow) that is hyperintense on T2-weighted image, an appearance typical of myxoma.
claims.locator: Atrial Myxoma (Cardiac MRI Scan) image caption

claims.text: Anemia, thrombocytopenia and elevated WBC, ESR, CRP and gamma-globulins are common; ECG may show left atrial enlargement
claims.quote: Anemia; thrombocytopenia; and elevation of white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and gamma-globulins are common. ECG may show left atrial enlargement.

claims.text: Causes Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor (45 to 85%); incidence in females is 2 to 3 times that in males (males more often in the uncommon familial Carney complex); most occur in the left atrium
claims.quote: Myxoma is most common (2), accounting for 45 to 85% of all primary cardiac tumors (3, 4). Incidence in females is 2 to 3 times that in males (5, 6). In uncommon familial forms (Carney complex), males are affected more often. Most myxomas occur in the left atrium (3), and the rest occur in the other chambers as a solitary tumor or, less commonly, at several sites.

claims.text: Most are pedunculated and may prolapse through the mitral valve and obstruct ventricular filling during diastole; friable, irregular myxomas increase the risk of systemic embolism
claims.quote: Most are pedunculated and may prolapse through the mitral valve and obstruct ventricular filling during diastole. The remainder of the tumors are broad-based and sessile. Myxomas may be myxoid and gelatinous; smooth, firm, and lobular; or friable and irregular. Friable, irregular myxomas increase risk of systemic embolism.

claims.text: Carney complex: a familial, autosomal dominant syndrome of recurrent cardiac myxomas with some combination of cutaneous myxomas, pigmented skin lesions, multiple endocrine neoplasia and other lesions; patients are often young (median age 25 to 29 years) with multiple myxomas and a higher recurrence risk
claims.quote: Carney complex is a familial, autosomal dominant syndrome of recurrent cardiac myxomas with some combination of cutaneous myxomas, myxoid mammary fibroadenomas, pigmented skin lesions (lentigines, ephelides, blue nevi), multiple endocrine neoplasia (primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease causing Cushing syndrome, growth hormone and prolactin-producing pituitary adenoma, testicular tumors, thyroid adenoma or carcinoma, and ovarian cysts), psammomatous melanotic schwannoma, breast ductal adenoma, and osteochondromyxoma. Patients are often young at presentation (median age, 25 to 29 years) (7), have multiple myxomas (particularly in the ventricles), and have a higher risk of myxoma recurrence.

claims.text: Symptoms May manifest with the triad of heart failure, embolic disease and constitutional symptoms
claims.quote: Myxomas may manifest with the triad of heart failure, embolic disease, and constitutional symptoms.

claims.text: May cause a diastolic murmur that mimics mitral stenosis but whose loudness and location vary beat to beat with body position; approximately 15% of pedunculated LA myxomas produce an audible “tumor plop” as they drop into the mitral orifice during diastole
claims.quote: Myxomas may cause a diastolic murmur that mimics the murmur of mitral stenosis but whose loudness and location vary from beat to beat with body position. Approximately 15% of pedunculated left atrial myxomas produce an audible “tumor plop” as they drop into the mitral orifice during diastole (1).

claims.text: With some tumors (especially gelatinous myxomas), thrombi or tumor fragments may embolize systemically (eg, brain, coronary arteries, kidneys, spleen, extremities) or to the lungs
claims.quote: With some tumors (especially gelatinous myxomas), thrombi or tumor fragments may embolize into the systemic circulation (eg, brain, coronary arteries, kidneys, spleen, extremities) or the lungs and cause manifestations specific to those organs.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: surgical excision

Benign primary tumors: generally surgical excision followed by serial echo or other imaging to monitor for recurrence, unless another disorder (eg, dementia) contraindicates surgery; surgery is usually curative
claims.quote: Treatment of benign primary tumors is generally surgical excision followed by serial echocardiography or other imaging to monitor for recurrence. Tumors are excised unless another disorder (eg, dementia) contraindicates surgery. Surgery is usually curative (eg, in one series, survival rates were 96% at 1 year and 75% at 10 years [2]).
